title: SHAIKH v IKIA LIMITED and Ors
text:
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
AUCKLAND
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TAMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE
[2026] NZERA 510
3465964
BETWEEN HASMAT SHAIKH
Applicant
AND IKIA LIMITED
First Respondent
PUSVIK LIMITED
Second Respondent
ANURAG GUPTA
Third Respondent
Member of Authority: Marija Urlich
Representatives: Mohammed Shahadat, counsel for the Applicant
Anurag Gupta, in person and director of the Second and
Third Respondents
Investigation Meeting: On the papers
Determination: 30 July 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment Relationship Problem
[1] Hasmat Shaikh worked for Ikia Limited (Ikia) as a chef from 15 January 2025
until 19 October 2025. He seeks orders for payment of holiday pay and alternative pay
due when his employment ended. Reimbursement of the filing fee is also sought.
[2] Ikia, Pusvik Limited and Mr Gupta have not lodged statements in reply in the
required form.1 Mr Gupta accepted service on behalf of the respondents and has
1 Employment Relations Authority Regulations 2000, clause 8.

acknowledged arrears are due Mr Shaikh. He says the amount is less than claimed
because from 2 June 2025 Mr Shaikh agreed to work three hours less per week.
The Authority’s investigation
[3] On 16 May 2026 Mr Shaikh filed a statement of problem in the Authority. On
18 May 2026 the statement of problem was served on the respondents, Mr Gupta having
advised he would accept service by email on their behalf. As stated above the
respondents did not lodge statements in reply in the required form.
[4] To progress the matter, by directions dated 8 July 2026 the Authority identified
the issues to be investigated and determined and directed the parties file any relevant
information in affidavit form by 17 July 2026. The directions were emailed to the
parties at the addresses with which they have corresponded with the Authority. In
addition, the directions and statement of problem were couriered to the directors of Ikia
and Pusvik Limited and to Mr Gupta personally at the address for service provided in
the companies register for that purpose.
[5] In accordance with the timetable directions on 17 July 2026 Mr Shaikh filed an
affidavit in support of his claim. On the same day Mr Gupta emailed the Authority
including acknowledgement that “holiday pay is owing” but that the sum is less than
claimed because the parties agreed to reduce Mr Shaihk’s hours of work due to business
downturn. Correspondence between the parties was attached. Mr Shaikh through his
representative provided a response. The Authority then emailed the parties at my
direction that I wished to move to determine the matter and provided the respondents a
further opportunity to file supporting information including that it should be in affidavit
form by close of business Friday 24 July 2026. Mr Gupta provided further information.
I am satisfied the parties have had a fair opportunity to provide relevant information to
the Authority and that it is appropriate to determine this employment relationship
problem on the information before the Authority.
[6] As permitted by s 174E of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) this
determination has stated findings of fact and law, expressed conclusions on issues
necessary to dispose of the matter and specified orders made. It has not recorded all
evidence and information received.

Issues
[7] The issues identified for investigation and determination are whether:
(i) Hasmat Shaikh is owed $2,400 (gross) in holiday pay arrears and $1,575
(gross) in alternative holiday pay for public holidays worked?
(ii) If so, are the respondents’ jointly and severally liable for the arrears?
(iii) Interest should be awarded on unpaid arrears? and
(iv) Hasmat Shaikh is entitled to recover the Authority filing fee of $71.55?
Discussion
Are arrears of holiday pay and alternative holiday pay due and owing?
[8] As an employee Mr Shaikh was entitled to holiday and alternative holiday pay
calculated and paid when his employment ended.2 There is no dispute Mr Shaikh has
not been paid termination holiday or alternative holiday pay. He has sought payment of
these arrears since his employment ended. What is disputed is the sum owed. It is
necessary to record Mr Shiekh sought through his representative wage, time and leave
records and Ikia Limited does not appear to have provided them on request as it is
required under law.3 No penalty is sought.
[9] The parties’ written employment agreement (the IEA) entered on 20 January
2025 provides Mr Shaikh would be paid $25 (gross) per hour for 30 hours per week.
Mr Shiek’s information is that he worked 5 days per week. The IEA also provides any
changes to the terms contained therein must be in writing and agreed by both employer
and employee. I am satisfied Mr Shaikh worked the 7 public holidays he has averred to
during this employment and that he has not been paid the public holiday loading for the
hours worked on those days or been paid the alternative holidays. I am further satisfied
he has not received termination holiday pay to which he was entitled calculated at 8%
of total earnings.4
[11] Mr Gupta says the parties agreed to reduce Mr Shaikh’s hours by 3 per week
with concomitant reduction in wages. He relies on an email dated 8 June 2025 to Mr
Gupta. The email does not establish the parties agreed to reduce Mr Shaikh’s hours of
2 Holidays Act 2003, ss 27 and 60.
3 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 130(2).
4 Holidays Act 2003, s 23.

work by 3 per week or his pay. It records that a proposal was put to Mr Shaik to reduce
his hours by 3 per week in response to business decline. This email followed Mr Shaikh
emailing Mr Gupta on 2 June asking for his payslip for the week before, reminding him
he was entitled to time and a half for work on public holidays and listing the 6 public
holidays he had worked to date that year in relation to which the email states “you
haven’t paid me anything”.5
[12] Mr Gupta’s 8 June email does not record Mr Sheikh agreed to the proposal to
reduce his hours and there is no subsequent written record of such an agreement. It is
more likely than not Mr Shaikh did not agree to reduce his hours and pay because Mr
Shaihk’s pay did not reduce. What the subsequent emails show is the employer went
ahead with the proposal and made up the 3-hours per week pay using Mr Shaihk’s
holiday pay entitlement. On 6 July Mr Gupta emailed him recording Mr Shaikh’s public
holiday pay entitlement had been used to top up 9 hours between 9 June and 29 June.
On 22 August Mr Gupta emailed Mr Shaikh advising him for the period 30 June to 27
July 12 hours of “public holiday owing hours” had been used towards his pay. Mr Gupta
referred to this in an email to Mr Shaikh after his employment ended and in response to
Mr Shaikh’s request for arrears to be paid.
[13] I note the employment agreement expressly deals with how alternative holidays
might be taken including that it would be a day off.6 This is consistent with the Holidays
Act which provides an alternative holiday must be a whole working day off work.7
Even if an hourly arrangement could lawfully be entered it is doubtful parties could
lawfully agree to use alternative holiday entitlement to maintain agreed weekly pay.
[14] Mr Shaikh is entitled to arrears of holiday pay of $2,382.00 (gross)8 and
alternative holiday pay of $1,575.00 (gross).9
5 I am satisfied Mr Shiekh was not paid the T1/2 loading for public holidays worked and that the
respondents are on notice of this because it is part of the calculation Mr Shiekh has described as
alternative holiday pay.
6 IEA page 10.
7 Holidays Act 2003, s 57.
8 8% of total earnings of $29,777 (refer IRD records $29,250 (gross) + $525) = $2,382.
9 Public holiday pay loading $525 (7 x public holidays T1/2) + 7 x alternative holidays at $150 (gross)
per day = $1575 (gross).

Who owes the arrears?
[15] Mr Shaikh seeks orders jointly and severally against Ikia Limited, Pusvik
Limited and Mr Gupta personally. He says because his IRD records show Pushvik
Limited paid his wages between April and July 2025 it may have become his employer.
This is not accepted. The employing entity is Ikia Limited, as recorded in the IEA and
it has paid the balance of Mr Shaikh’s wages. Any arrangement between Ikia Limited
and Pusvik Limited regarding payment of wages in the identified period is unknown to
the Authority but, in the absence of clear evidence Pusvik Limited acted as an employer
the claim against it is unestablished.
[16] Ikia Limited owes Mr Shaikh the arrears at [14] above. It is to pay him those
sums totalling $3,957.00 (gross) within 14 days of the date of this determination.
[17] Mr Gupta is the sole director of Ikia Limited. The information before the
Authority shows he was involved in matters concerning Mr Shaikh’s employment – Mr
Gupta signed the IEA on behalf of Ikia Limited in his capacity as director of that entity
and Mr Gupta has been involved in matters concerning Mr Shaihk’s pay including
corresponding with him about his holiday pay entitlement being used to top up his
wages. I am satisfied, on the information before the Authority Mr Gupta may well meet
the requirements of a person involved which would allow Mr Shaikh to recover
categories of minimum entitlements such as holiday pay and alternative holiday pay
from Mr Gupta personally.10
[18] However, Ikia Limited may still pay those sums. It continues to trade and
remains on the companies register. Default as required for a s 142Y application is not
established.
[19] If Ikia Limited does not pay Mr Shaikh the arrears as ordered, Mr Shaikh has
leave to seek to recover the defaulted sum from Mr Gupta personally.
Interest
[20] It is appropriate where a person has been deprived of the use of money to make
an award for interest. Mr Shaikh is entitled to an award of interest on the total order of
